extracted.intended_audience: journalists, press-freedom advocates, legal observers, and general readers interested in legal protections and prosecutions involving journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Documentation and reporting of incidents, arrests, and legal actions involving journalists and press freedom, with references to applicable U.S. statutes and case law. The page compiles events, reactions, and the legal standards cited in coverage of those incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bartnicki v. Vopper: disclosure protection
rubrics_metrics.description: A 2001 Supreme Court case Bartnicki v. Vopper established protections for "a person's right to disclose illegally intercepted communications if they were not part of the illegal interception itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This precedent is cited as a protection for journalists or others who publish illegally intercepted communications provided they were not complicit in the illegal interception; useful in assessing whether publication of leaked/intercepted material is constitutionally protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy Protection Act of 1980: subpoena requirement for journalist work products
rubrics_metrics.description: The Privacy Protection Act of 1980 requires the government to get a subpoena to obtain journalist work products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute limits searches/seizures of newsroom materials and generally requires the government to use subpoenas rather than search warrants to obtain reporters' materials; cited as a statutory protection that can constrain investigative searches of journalists' homes/offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Espionage Act of 1917: restrictions on national defense information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Espionage Act of 1917 makes it illegal to obtain information relating to national defense with the intent of using that information against the United States for the gain of any foreign nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act can be invoked in prosecutions involving classified or national defense information and is often raised as a counterweight to disclosure protections; assessing intent and nature of the information is key when applying this statute to journalists or sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act (FACE Act) — 18 U.S.C. §248
rubrics_metrics.description: The FACE Act (codified at 18 U.S.C. §248) prohibits the use of force, threat of force, or physical obstruction to interfere with a person's exercise of religious worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutors considered charging a journalist under this statute in connection with a protest inside a church; the statute is relevant when alleged conduct involves physical obstruction or force at places of worship even if the defendant claims to be reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18 U.S.C. §241: civil rights conspiracy statute
rubrics_metrics.description: 18 U.S.C. §241 is a Reconstruction-era civil rights conspiracy statute commonly associated with the Ku Klux Klan Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statute can be used to charge conspiracies to deprive persons of constitutional rights; prosecutors' consideration of this statute signals potential charging strategies when allegations involve coordinated interference with civil rights (e.g., rights to assembly, religious exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable cause requirement for magistrate approval of criminal complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal magistrate judge declined to approve the proposed criminal complaint, saying the government had not presented sufficient probable cause at that stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial review for probable cause is a procedural threshold before arrest/charging; absence of sufficient probable cause at the magistrate stage can block or delay criminal complaints — an important protection and evaluative standard in cases against journalists or others.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment protection for journalistic conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendants (and their attorneys) may argue that journalistic conduct is protected by the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether particular on-the-ground actions (e.g., livestreaming a protest inside a church) are protected speech/press activity depends on context and competing legal claims (e.g., trespass, obstruction, force). The First Amendment defense is a central evaluative consideration in prosecutions involving reporters.
